title: Four games and editor controls for reading the final image

scenes.title: appearance-prerequisite
lines: Compare the same responsibility across different games. The first three sources are March2026 DLSS5 previews. Read Off and On first, then examine the light on faces and clothing. The September basketball release is a separate example.

scenes.title: appearance-resident
lines: Start with Resident Evil, moving from a dark room to the rainy vehicle shot. Watch the turning face and wet clothing. The labelled On condition changes their surface appearance. Different poses are not a pixel-aligned ground truth.

scenes.title: appearance-starfield
lines: Starfield provides an orange coat and suits in brighter interiors. The dialogue UI identifies a character; it is not a quality score. Lighting differs from the rainy scene, but the question remains: where does the final appearance of light on skin and fabric change?

scenes.title: appearance-hogwarts
lines: Hogwarts Legacy moves through an interior, a street and an underground shot. At each cut, select the new face and clothing. Compare Off and On within that shot. A glowing wand or visible steam alone does not establish new physical simulation.

scenes.title: appearance-nba
lines: Now examine skin, jerseys and arm highlights on the basketball court. The close Detroit number-two shot changes from Off to On; subsequent dunks use other camera angles. This compares displayed appearance, not ball physics or input response. Compare those surfaces with dark wet clothing, a bright coat and underground fabric: the same display-stage task meets different surface conditions.

scenes.title: appearance-to-controls
lines: We compared surface appearance across four games. Next, control a cause directly: exposure and focus can change the image without moving lights. Connect editor settings to results, then inspect the actual resources inside a frame.

scenes.title: exposure-context
lines: This is a2017 Unreal editor demonstration. Separate the cube arrangement from the post-process controls on the right. Camera and parameters both change, so we first identify the edited inputs rather than attributing every brightness difference to one feature.

scenes.title: exposure-after-limit
lines: The exposure panel shows lower and upper brightness limits and a bias. Reading those settings differs from measuring displayed pixel intensity. Keep the same bright and dark cube faces in view while following the changes.

scenes.title: histogram-open
lines: The demonstration switches to histogram visualization. It adds information for reading a brightness distribution instead of showing only the ordinary image. Connect the lower graph to the controls. Its green and blue colors are visualization, not the wall material colors.

scenes.title: histogram-log-scale
lines: The visualization explicitly names a logarithmic scale. Equal horizontal spacing does not mean an equal additive brightness change. It displays a wide dark-to-bright range in one view. Read the scale before relating graph position to brightness.

scenes.title: histogram-camera-condition
lines: Camera movement changes the proportions of surfaces in the image. Seeing more bright cubes can change the brightness distribution within the same lit scene. Exposure comparisons therefore need camera framing as well as settings. This is an observation demonstration, not a fixed-camera numerical experiment.

scenes.title: histogram-control-result
lines: We can now separate three roles: edited settings, diagnostic visualization and the final image. Settings are inputs; the graph helps inspection; the displayed image includes later display processing. A diagnostic graph color is not itself a final surface pixel color.

scenes.title: bloom-surface
lines: In the bloom controls, distinguish spread around bright regions from the cube surfaces themselves. A wider glow and light bouncing onto another surface answer different questions. Inspect the edited effect rather than treating a bright impression as proof of an indirect-lighting implementation.

scenes.title: tone-range
lines: Next come color and tone controls. The cubes remain while their displayed appearance can be adjusted. Earlier chapters created scene lighting; this stage maps its result into a display range. Distinguish computing the input from shaping its presentation.

scenes.title: tone-highlight-reference
lines: Use both a bright face and a shaded face on the same cube. Looking only at highlights can miss contrast changes; looking only at shadows can miss highlight compression. Follow the control and both regions to distinguish overall changes from changes concentrated in a brightness range.

scenes.title: tone-material-distinction
lines: A darker-looking surface does not by itself establish that its material asset changed. Here we observe post-process controls and their results. A claim about material inputs requires inspecting those inputs separately. Similar image changes can originate at different stages.

scenes.title: grade-channel-controls
lines: Read brightness and color balance as separate aspects of grading. Keep the cube arrangement as a reference and identify the chosen control. A warmer or cooler appearance can resemble a changed light color without establishing the same underlying operation.

scenes.title: grade-shared-reference
lines: Keeping the same surface preserves a reference for comparison. Red follows the observed face; another color identifies the setting. The mark is an observation location, not a game-world distance or physical unit. Reacquire the surface when the camera changes.

scenes.title: grade-to-lookup
lines: Record the edited input, the surface where a change appears and any simultaneous condition changes. Next we examine a separate color-transform resource, continuing the distinction between final displayed color and the original lighting value.

scenes.title: lookup-resource
lines: First locate the setting that will apply the color transform. The demonstrator selects the area labelled Post Process Blendable and searches for blend in the right panel. The scene cubes and the effect settings have separate roles. Establish where the next resource will be connected.

scenes.title: lookup-endpoint
lines: The panel shows a post-process material entry, followed by a lookup-table asset displayed as a strip of colors, or LUT. It represents color correspondence rather than a small map of the game world. After identifying the color resource, distinguish distance and focus in the same cube arrangement.

scenes.title: focus-legend-context
lines: Read the focus legend first: blue marks far regions, green near regions and black the focused region. These are not cube material colors. As distance and transition settings are edited, distinguish the focus reference from the width of its transition.

scenes.title: focus-distance-transition
lines: Focus distance and transition width are not the same quantity. One establishes a reference location; the other relates to the surrounding change range. Read the edited field before inspecting the affected regions, without pairing different settings as an identical-condition On/Off comparison.

scenes.title: focus-normal-return
lines: Back in the ordinary view, a nearer cube appears blurred. Separate diagnostic colors from ordinary scene colors. Camera and focus-related settings also change in this demonstration, so record those conditions when explaining the blur.

scenes.title: focus-error-isolation
lines: When focus effects are enabled during reconstruction comparisons, a blurred edge can be misattributed. Check focus and camera conditions first, then the reconstruction conditions. Separating stages lets similar-looking blur be explained by different causes.

scenes.title: focus-later-settings
lines: The later editor interval retains the cube arrangement as a reference. Follow the selected control and compare near and far surfaces. An overall impression of blur can hide which distance region changed. Separating the focus reference and its surrounding regions makes the observation more specific.

scenes.title: focus-observation-protocol
lines: Read the input name, locate its change, then inspect the affected surface. Record camera changes separately. This observation method transfers to other engines without assuming their internal post-process order is identical.

scenes.title: focus-to-frame-inspection
lines: We compared final appearance in four games with editor exposure, color and focus controls. We can observe changes, but identifying which command read which resource is another question. Frame inspection now follows actual inputs and outputs rather than relying on feature names.

scenes.title: capture-context
lines: This is our channel’s simple DirectX12 demonstration, not evidence of a complex game lighting implementation. Separate the frame inspection window from its event list and follow how selecting an operation exposes different data. We connect a visible shape with the command that produced it.

scenes.title: capture-event-purpose
lines: Event names guide inspection. Clearing an image and drawing a triangle have different roles. Start with the result being investigated, then select its producing operation. An item appearing in a list does not establish that it affected every pixel.

scenes.title: capture-target-view
lines: Selecting DrawInstanced exposes a colored triangle on the blue background, unlike the clear operation. Identify the selected command’s output first, then move to mesh vertices and shader inputs. The investigation moves from the output image to its input data.

scenes.title: capture-position-input
lines: Separate position from color in the mesh and input views. Positions relate to triangle shape, while color inputs can affect appearance. A color table does not reveal every lighting quantity. First match the selected command to its shader input names.

scenes.title: capture-stage-selection
lines: A return value means different things at different shader stages. Do not describe a vertex-shader return as the pixel shader’s final color. Read the selected stage and input, then connect to the retained color-return demonstration. Resource names and producing operations provide more concrete evidence than appearance alone.

scenes.title: resource-viewer-context
lines: Switch to Unreal’s resource viewer. Several names appear, but they do not all describe the same texture. Distinguish a shadow-page pool from a virtual-texture physical pool. The earlier page discussion now connects to locating actual resources in the viewer.

scenes.title: resource-name-limits
lines: After locating a name, inspect dimensions and usage. Lumen radiance data and shadow data should not be collapsed into one generic light resource. Names start the investigation; producers and consumers complete it. This viewer alone does not verify every dependency in the frame.

scenes.title: resource-upload-control
lines: The next control concerns virtual-texture uploads. The word frame in its name does not make it frame generation. Identify the data being handled before relating the setting to the visible response. Performance-related numbers mean different things depending on which task receives the budget.

scenes.title: resource-budget-to-measure
lines: How quickly resources upload and how quickly a frame renders are different measurements. Record cache, loading and camera conditions. Having connected the resource view to its controls, the retained performance discussion now uses conditions and repeated measurements rather than one instantaneous number.
